headings.title: Introduction and Functional Anatomy of Coronary Vessels
headings.content:
The heart is a hardworking muscular pump that beats continuously, yet the blood sitting inside its own chambers cannot nourish the thick myocardial walls. Instead, the myocardium relies entirely on the **coronary circulation** network, a dedicated vascular system branching directly off the aorta.

- **Right Coronary Artery (RCA)**: Travels along the coronary sulcus, supplying the right atrium, right ventricle, and frequently the inferior wall of the left ventricle along with the conduction system.
- **Left Main Coronary Artery**: A short trunk that quickly splits into the **Left Anterior Descending (LAD)** artery, which feeds the front and bottom of the left ventricle, and the **Circumflex artery**, which wraps around the lateral wall.
- **Coronary Sinus**: The primary venous collector resting on the posterior heart surface, receiving deoxygenated blood from smaller cardiac veins before emptying directly into the right atrium.

headings.title: Myocardial Perfusion Mechanics and Diastole
headings.content:
Unlike skeletal muscle or other visceral organs that receive blood flow continuously during contraction, the heart muscle squeezes its own blood vessels shut when it contracts. During **systole**, intense myocardial intramyocardial pressure collapses the small coronary capillaries, temporarily halting forward flow. 

Consequently, the vast majority of coronary blood flow and myocardial perfusion happens during **diastole**, when the heart relaxes and the aortic valve closes. This physiological reality creates a strict dependence on heart rate. If a patient develops severe tachycardia, the diastolic phase shortens drastically, leaving very little time for blood to flow through the coronary bed and threatening the subendocardium with ischemia.

headings.title: Physiological Regulation of Coronary Blood Flow
headings.content:
The heart demands an immediate adjustment in blood supply whenever metabolic activity changes. Under normal resting conditions, the myocardium extracts nearly 75% of the oxygen delivered by the blood, meaning it cannot simply extract more oxygen when workload increases; it must increase blood flow instead.

Local metabolic control is the dominant regulator. When myocardial oxygen demand rises, tissue cells release adenosine, hydrogen ions, and carbon dioxide. These metabolites cause direct **vasodilation** of the coronary arterioles, lowering resistance and allowing a surge of fresh blood. Autonomic neural input also modulates this flow, with sympathetic stimulation causing both vasoconstriction via alpha receptors and metabolic vasodilation via beta receptors.

headings.title: Pathophysiology of Coronary Artery Disease and Ischemia
headings.content:
When lipid plaques build up inside the epicardial coronary arteries, a pathological process known as **atherosclerosis** develops. As these plaques enlarge, they narrow the vessel lumen and restrict the maximum volume of blood that can reach the myocardial tissue during exertion.

When blood supply fails to meet metabolic demand, **myocardial ischemia** occurs. This temporary oxygen deprivation alters cellular metabolism, forcing a shift to anaerobic pathways that rapidly accumulate lactic acid and trigger chest discomfort, or **angina pectoris**. If a plaque ruptures completely and forms an occlusive thrombus, blood flow stops entirely, leading to cellular death, or myocardial infarction.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content:
Detecting compromised coronary circulation requires a combination of thorough patient history, physical examination, and specialized diagnostic testing. Nurses must carefully evaluate the characteristics of chest pain, noting factors like location, radiation to the jaw or left arm, and precipitating triggers.

- **12-Lead Electrocardiogram (ECG)**: Identifies acute electrical changes, such as ST-segment elevation or T-wave inversion, indicating ischemia or injury.
- **Cardiac Biomarkers**: Blood tests like troponin measure intracellular proteins released into the bloodstream when myocardial cells undergo necrosis.
- **Coronary Angiography**: The gold standard imaging test where a radiopaque dye is injected into the coronary arteries via catheterization to visualize exact blockage sites.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Management
headings.content:
Managing a patient with impaired coronary circulation focuses on restoring the balance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand while protecting threatened tissue. Nurses coordinate immediate pharmacological therapy and monitor vital signs closely.

Sublingual **nitroglycerin** is frequently administered to dilate peripheral and coronary vessels, reducing cardiac workload and increasing blood flow. Supplemental oxygen is provided if oxygen saturation falls below standard thresholds. Beyond acute care, nurses play a vital role in lifestyle education, helping patients modify risk factors such as hypertension, smoking, and poor diet to prevent further atherosclerotic progression.
